speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: RATIONING
subtopic: ADDITIONAL CHARGE BY PUBLIC CATERERS FOR TEA, COFFEE OR MILK
speechtext:
I should like to give an answer to a question asked by the hon. member for St. John-Albert (Mr. Hazen) on Monday, March 1. I should have taken the point of order that this question ought to have been placed on the order paper, but I did not do so. I would have done so if I had had time to give adequate consideration to it. However, this is the answer:

On Monday last the hon. member for St. John-Albert quoted a press dispatch respecting a recent order of the wartime prices and trade board permitting public caterers to charge five cents extra for non-alcoholic beverages served with meals, and asked me to inform the house what purpose this order is intended to serve.
Public caterers purvey nothing but foods, and since the basic period have borne the "squeeze" incident to the higher cost of foods, with respect to some of which there is no ceiling. The business is highly competitive and has never been regarded as a highly profitable one. The situation had become almost impossible for many of the smaller restaurants, and the board, after full investigation, decided that some relief would have to be given in order to maintain the essential service which is provided. It was felt that the situation was not one in which a subsidy could be recommended. The solution found avoided an over-all increase in the price of restaurant meals and gives the customer a chance to decide whether or not he wishes to add to the cost of his meal, or to give up the beverage on which the price increase has been granted.
An additional consideration was, of course, that the order should have the effect of conserving tea and coffee, for which ration coupons are not demanded from the consumer in restaurants.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext:
Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide, inter alia,
1.	That sums not exceeding $3,890,000,000 be granted to His Majesty towards defraying any expenses or making any advances or loans that may be incurred or granted by or under the authority of the governor in council during the year ending March 31, 1944, for-
(a)	the security, defence, peace, order and welfare of Canada;
(b)	the conduct of naval, military and air operations in or beyond Canada;
(c)	promoting the continuance of trade, industry and business communications, whether by means of insurance or indemnity against war risk or in any other manner whatsoever; and
(d)	the carrying out of any measures deemed necessary or advisable by the governor in council in consequence of the existence of a state of war.
2.	That the governor in council be empowered to raise by way of loan under the provisions of the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act, 1931, such sum or sums of money, not exceeding in the whole the sum of $3,890,000,000 as may be required for the purpose of defraying such
expenses or making such advances or loans, the principal and interest of any such loan to be a charge upon and payable out of the consolidated revenue fund.
3.	That the governor in council be empowered to reexpend, advance or loan moneys that may be received by way of refund or repayment of advances, loans or expenditure under the War Appropriation Acts of 1939 (second session), 1940, 1941, 1942 and 1943.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this resolution asks for authority to introduce a bill which is designed to provide the appropriation we shall require for war expenditures during the fiscal year 1943-44. The bill will be in exactly the same form as the main war appropriation of last year except for the amount of the vote to be asked for.
The magnitude of this vote and the fact that it is to provide for our direct war financial programme for the new year makes this by far the most important measure with which the house will have to deal during the present session. It will provide an opportunity for discussing and appraising not only the war programme which we are proposing for next year, but also the record of war activities and expenditures during the fiscal year now drawing to a close. In view of the courtesy of the house in refraining from extended debate on the supplementary war appropriation which was voted a week or ten days ago, every opportunity will be given to hon. members to make such inquiries and comments as they may wish to make in regard to the expenditures of the current year.

It will be noted that, in round numbers, the aggregate expenditures of the three defence services are estimated at $3,320,000,000 for 1943-44 as compared with an estimated $1,913,000,000 for the current fiscal year. Breaking down these totals, we find that army services account for $1,764,000,000 in 1943-44 as compared with $1,061,000,000 in 1942-43; air services, $1,129,000,000 as compared with $627,000,000; naval services, $489,000,000 as compared with $208,000,000; and sundry services, $22,500,000 as compared with $17,600,000.
The substantial increase for the air services reflects not only the expansion of the air training plan and the increased air force activities on both coasts of Canada but also the acceptance by Canada of full responsibility for maintaining and equipping thirty-eight
Royal Canadian Air Force squadrons overseas and for the pay of all R.C.A.F. personnel overseas. In the naval estimates we see the effect not only of gradual expansion of our navy but also of the increased naval shipbuilding programme. The estimated increase in the expenditures of the army is accounted for not only by expanding programmes but by the substantial increase in deliveries of finished equipment and war supplies now coming from Canadian war plants and the probability of more active operations overseas. However, it would not be appropriate at this time, and I will not attempt to give detailed explanations for any of the increases or for the programme as a whole, because when the bill is before the house detailed estimates of the proposed expen-
War Appropriation

ditures by various departments and functions will be given by the ministers who are individually responsible.
In the case of the Department of Munitions and Supply the estimated net expenditure for 1943-44 is $166 million. This compares with an estimated expenditure for the current year of about $689 million. The latter figure, however, included $200 million for the purchase of the British interest in Canadian war plants and provided for an expansion of plant and equipment much larger than will be required during the coming year. For the war activities carried on by all other departments or agencies of government the estimate for 1943-44 is $254 million as compared with an estimated expenditure during the present year of $200 million. In this connection I may point out for the information of the house that the largest single item in this category is $120,000,000 to provide for subsidies under the Commodity Prices Stabilization corporation. In view of the recent clarification of functions in regard to subsidy payments as between the wartime prices and trade board and the Department of Agriculture, part of this requirement will be assigned to the Department of Agriculture, but it is not at the moment practical to make the allocation. The remaining $65 million requested by the appropriation is an estimate of the amount required to cover cash outlays charged to active assets rather than to expenditure, and for contingencies.
I shall not now say more about the details of these estimates by departments and functions. That would be needlessly confusing to the house, before it has had time to study and digest the salient features of the table which I have placed on Hansard. Nor do I think it is necessary to attempt at great length to consider these proposed war expenditures in the light of our over-all financial picture. I had an opportunity of doing that only last evening in the budget address. Let me touch very briefly on a few salient points and then examine in more detail one or two general points which have been raised in the house during the last few weeks.
In the first place, I wish to enphasize that Canada's war expenditure for 1943-44 is not covered by this war appropriation of $3,890,000,000. To that should be added the billion dollar appropriation to be requested in the mutual aid bill. It is the sum of these two appropriations which represents the estimated cost of our war programme for the new fiscal year. That sum is $4,890,000,000, which, hon. members will note, is almost eighty-nine per cent of the dominion's estimated aggregate expenditure for 1943-44. It

may be added that it is also nearly three times the estimated total cost of Canada's war effort during the great war 1914-18.
In the second place, I want to say that the total represents a very careful estimate of the cash outlays involved by the war effort which we believe we can accomplish during the twelve months beginning April 1 next. As I said last evening, it is not a financial programme but merely the financial counterpart of the physical or economic programme, the measure in dollar terms of the amount of man-power and resources which we believe we can throw into the war effort as our contribution to victory during the coming year. In the early years of the war the estimates of war expenditures in this country as in other countries tended to run ahead of actual accomplishments "because everybody tended to underestimate the time it takes to get plants built, production under way on a large scale, and organization completed. Even last year, as the house will remember, I asked for a war appropriation substantially less than the departments estimated they could spend, but I warned the house that I would probably have to come back before the end of the year for additional funds for our direct war expenditure as well as for additional funds to enable the United Kingdom to continue her purchases of foodstuffs, raw materials and munitions in this country. Actually the departments were able to spend all they estimated and, indeed, somewhat more in some instances. Our programme was expanded in accordance with changing conditions, and early this year we decided that it would be wiser for us to meet Britain's needs for dollars during the remainder of this year not by a further gift but by purchasing outright her interest in Canadian war plants and thus getting title and full control of these plants in the name of Canada. These things, therefore, are the explanation of the supplementary war appropriation of S858 million, and not as one hon. member has said, the lack of careful planning by the government with respect to war financial expenditures.
As time goes on, the tendency to which I have referred, of expenditures to lag behind estimates, disappears and a very substantial proportion of the increased expenditures for the new year estimated by the three defence services are based on the expectation of receiving largely expanded deliveries of mechanized equipment, munitions and supplies which mark the fruition of the able and aggressive planning of production by my colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe), and the capacity for

War Appropriation
achievement of Canadian business management and Canadian labour. As I have said, I think we can spend during the year all of the huge sums for which we are now asking, because I believe we can achieve the production of war goods and the diversion of manpower to the armed services which our programme calls for. I am asking for all I think we can spend, but I must add this, that if before the end of the year it should prove that we shall need something additional that will be because we have actually been able to divert more of our resources to the war effort.
There are some who think that we are trying to do too much, or even already doing too much, and that we are going to bankrupt the country. Well, I want to say that we cannot do too much; that nothing which the Canadian people can do is too much to throw into this struggle for the right to survive in freedom and decency; that the way to wreck this country and bankrupt civilization is for Canada and her partners to do just a little less than enough to win. Unless I am gravely mistaken, that truth is plainly evident to the Canadian people as a whole.

This bulletin shows that the war effort in the three countries is absorbing the national income according to the following percentages: United States, 24-5 per cent; Great Britain, 36-8 per cent, and Canada, 39-1 per cent. If these figures mean anything, and if I correctly interpret them, they show that the Canadian people are being asked by this government to contribute to the war effort a greater proportion of the national income than either our rich neighbours to the south or our very hard-pressed blood brothers overseas.

speechtext:
Oh, yes. I have looked up
that issue of the federal reserve bulletin, and I find that the article cited by the hon. member refers to taxes rather than to the amount of effort devoted to war purposes. I am surprised that the hon. member did not make this clear, because it is an important distinction and one that is sufficiently understandable that there should be no need for confusion.
I would not undertake to vouch for the accuracy of the figures quoted in respect of the United Kingdom and the United States. The publication in which they appear is a reliable one and the figures are carefully described and qualified. However, it would appear that in the case of Canada the figures for taxation and for national income are probably both a little on the low side, although the relationship between the two does not appear to be seriously in error, and although, furthermore, we cannot speak with any great assurance in regard to our own statistics of national income. I understand that efforts are being made to bring about substantial improvements in our own national income figures, and I hope that before long we can make comparisons of this kind with much more assurance.
However, the essential point is that the table throws no light at all on the relative proportions of their national incomes which the three countries are devoting to the war effort. They were talking about taxes; they were not talking about the relative parts of their production that they were devoting to the war effort. If the table has any significance it is as to the light which it throws on the financial policy of the three countries. In Canada, as the house knows full well, we have endeavoured to carry the "pay-as-we-go policy" as far as practicable, and in this I believe we have had a greater measure of success than most other countries. That is a reason for pride and rejoicing rather than a point to censure. Canadians will have many occasions in future years to look back on this record with satisfaction.
What is relevant for the point which the hon. member for York-Sunbury had in mind is a comparison of national incomes with total war expenditures rather than merely with the amount financed through taxation. Particularly in view of the state of our national income statistics, I would not wish to compare the three countries on this basis, even if we had such reliable figures, and I am not referring to statistics kept 'by any particular department, because several agencies of

War Appropriation

government are keeping national income statistics. In fact, it is extremely difficult to get an estimate which is accurate, and I think it is found that way in other countries, as well as in Canada. Even if we had such reliable figures, the subject is one which bristles with technical difficulties, and it is by no means easy to be certain that we are comparing like with like. Many qualifications would be required before we could get a proper basis of comparison. Let me give only one example. The rates of pay for the armed forces in the United Kingdom and in other European countries are substantially lower than our rates of pay. Consequently the expenditure upon pay and allowances for the armed forces of these countries is made to appear less in proportion than it is for us here , in North America, although in fact the proportion of man-power and of real economic resources may be higher. Hence war expenditures are by no means a reliable guide in themselves when one is making a comparison between different nations.
However, we do not need to attempt such complicated statistical comparisons to get at the real truth of the matter. As I pointed out in the budget, we do not need to go beyond Very elementary statistics or even common observation to realize that we on the home front in Canada are still away behind the people of Britain in the degree to which we have cut down our civilian consumption for the sake of the war effort. It is fantastic to say that the moderate decline we have suffered from the peak of war-time consumption, and the increase in the inconveniences we have suffered in shopping and travelling, compare with the belt-tightening and the personal sacrifices and hardships of the British people. Furthermore, we should want to make this type of comparison rather than compare what we have done with what has been achieved in the United States which was a neutral country prior to December 7, 1941. That country has been mobilizing with tremendous speed; it has pointed its sights very high indeed, and if it is able to translate into action the $108 billion budget for which the President has asked, we may have cause for envy rather than for self-complacency.
We are doing our utmost to avoid waste or extravagance and to get as much as we can for each dollar of expenditure. I realize that in an undertaking as vast as our war programme we cannot achieve perfection in this regard, but I feel that within the inevitable human limitations we are getting good value for our money. We have put into effect a great variety of controls over expenditure, and wherever we see, or someone tells us, that one

of the human cogs in a huge machine has slipped, we do our best to correct the mistake and safeguard against its recurrence. I try to avail myself of every opportunity for criticism of any expenditure that appears to be unessential or unnecessarily large, and I trust the house will do likewise. It is only by such self-criticism and such constant vigilance that we can secure economy and efficiency in any democratic, cooperative effort.
If, therefore, it be true that w'e are getting reasonable value for our money, it follows that those who argue that our war expenditures are drawn on too large a scale really mean that we are attempting to devote too much effort to the war. Apparently they wrant us to go slow, to limit our war effort, to cut down on man-power and materials. They want us to have a war effort under which we can all be comfortable rather than one which would stretch our energies and our resourcefulness to the limit. In this way they would seek to solve problems of shortages of butter and beef, and restaurant seats, and pullman cars. I for one do not believe that to be the wish of the Canadian people. That is not the type of war effort which would enable the Canadian people to hold their heads high in the family of nations. That is not the policy to -which the government and this country have committed themselves.
Finally, I turn more specifically to the question:	are we bankrupting the country?
The hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Lacroix) appeared to build up a bogey of the country somehow running out of money, of our coming to the end of our financial resources. That is a situation which might confront one individual, or a group within the community, or even a nation in regard to its resources of foreign exchange; it is not a situation which confronts a nation in regard to its own production and internal financing. We do not pay for the war out of some hoard of money that we have accumulated in the past. We pay for it out of the taxes and savings that we obtain from the current income of the whole nation. We shall not run short of money. Indeed, our danger is the very reverse of that, namely, that we may pile up too much money in the pockets and bank accounts of Canadians, unless we strive with every effort to promote the sale of victory bonds and war savings certificates.	[DOT]
If we are bankrupting the nation, is it not indeed a strange type of bankruptcy? How can we use such a term to describe the process under which this country has doubled its national income in three years, has wiped out unemployment, has multiplied its production of many things and learned many types of new

Social Security
skills, has expanded and diversified its production equipment, has multiplied its governmental revenues by more than four times, has enabled millions of its citizens to acquire a nest-egg for the future, has mobilized its full strength as a producing machine, and has developed a sense of productive achievement not hitherto known? No country goes bankrupt in this way; no country goes bankrupt by increasing its production and devoting part or all, or more than all of that increase to a supreme cause.
Of course our huge war expenditures do pose difficult financial problems during the war, and as I have often stated they make careful economic and financial management imperative. They involve a very large increase in our national debt, but it is a debt which we owe to ourselves, and it will be well within our capacity to manage if we follow sound policies. They make high taxes necessary if' we are to share the financial burdens and the real burdens fairly and effectively. But these taxes are essentially just a reflection in financial terms of the inevitable sacrifices of goods and services which we must make if we are to wage war on the scale that is necessary to defeat the enemy, and defeat him with the least possible loss of life. Given the scale of our national war effort in terms of men and materials, lower taxes would mean only that we would have a less equitable distribution of the burden, more danger of inflation, more danger of a break-down in our economic controls. Willingness to accept high taxes and other ' controls; willingness to deny ourselves now in order to avoid greater self-denial tomorrow is not really a test of the strength of our war spirit or the size of our war effort, but rather a test of our intelligence and foresight in allocating the burden of the cost of war.
Let those of us who are inclined to fear the economic consequences of our war expenditures remember that these expenditures have 'developed and brought to light an enormous increase in our Canadian capacity to produce-an increase greater than any of us had ever before suspected. Let them think of the future in terms of maintaining and still further developing that enlarged capacity, that potential of a greater national income. We can and must make use of that increased capacity after the war. We must develop that potential to the maximum. If we do, we can develop a far higher standard of living for the average Canadian than he has ever known before and with these higher incomes we can readily carry any debt, any debt to ourselves, that we shall accumulate

during the war. Our war expenditures are both a great medium of national achievement and a great investment in our own freedom and future. To suggest that they will bankrupt Canada is to suggest that Canadians lack ability and good sense to make intelligent use of their own future. I am not so lacking in faith in the mental and moral qualities of our own people.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON NATIONAL SOCIAL INSURANCE

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON NATIONAL SOCIAL INSURANCE
speechtext:
That a select committee of this house be appointed to examine and report on a national plan of social insurance which will constitute a charter of social security for the whole of Canada, and, to that end,
To examine and study the existing social insurance legislation of the parliament of Canada and of the several provincial legislatures; social insurance policies of other countries; the most practicable measures of social insurance for Canada,' including health insurance, and the steps which will be required to effect their inclusion in a national plan; the constitutional and financial adjustments which will be required for the achievement of a nation-wide plan of social security; and other related matters.
That the said committee have power to appoint, from among its members, such subcommittees as may be deemed advisable or necessary to deal with specific phases of the problems aforesaid, and call for persons, papers, and records, to print such papers and evidence from day to day as may be ordered by the committee for the use of the committee and members of the house; that the said committee report to the house from time to time; and that the said committee shall consist of the following members: Messieurs Adamson, Blanchette, Bourget, Breithaupt, Bruce, Casselman (Mrs.) (Edmonton East), Claxton, Cleaver, Cote, Diefenbaker, Donnelly, Fauteux, Gershaw, Gregory, Hatfield, Howden, Hurtubise, Johnston (Bow River), Kinley, Lalonde, Leclerc, Lockhart, Maelnnis, MacKenzie (Neepawa), Mackenzie (Vancouver Centre), MacKinnon (Kootenay East), Macmillan, McCann, McGarry, McGregor, McTlraith. Mayhew, Mitchell, Picard, Shaw, Slaght, Telford, Veniot. Warren, Wood, Wright, and that the provisions of standing order G5, limiting the number of members on special committees, be suspended in relation thereto.
Social Security

He said: Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of the session my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon), expressed the hope that the government would establish the various committees as early in the session as possible. On a subsequent day my hon. friend made particular reference to the committee on social security. He will agree I think that his wishes have been met as far as it was possible for the government to meet them. All standing and special committees of the house have now been established with the exception of this one and two others, notices of which appear on the order paper.
I should like to point out that in respect to the establishment of committees a new custom seems to be growing up in the house- I do not think it existed to any extent in previous parliaments-of having a lengthy debate at the time the resolution is moved. The custom in the past has been, unless strong exception were taken for some reason or other to a committee being appointed, to have the committees appointed practically without discussion. I am not taking exception to the tendency to debate at length resolutions for the appointment of committees but wish to make it clear that it is a departure, and also that it does take up a very considerable amount of the time of the house. The discussion of the subject referred to a committee usually takes place when the committee has made its report. I realize that in some sessions the reports have been late in coming down and probably hon. members have had that in mind in wishing to discuss some of these subjects at an earlier stage.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON NATIONAL SOCIAL INSURANCE
speechtext: Many of the reports are never discussed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON NATIONAL SOCIAL INSURANCE
speechtext:
There have been cases where that has happened. However, this year the committees will have been established at an early stage of the session and I hope will be able to report in plenty of time for such discussion as hon. members may wish to have.
I have a second reason for not wishing to discuss this resolution at any length at this stage.' It is that hon. members have already devoted a very considerable time to the resolution dealing with reestablishment and reconstruction. I believe all hon. members are interested in matters pertaining to post-war conditions and to a better social order and have felt that they would wish to place on Hansard their views with respect to some of the features of the new social order and some of the reforms which they feel should be speedily introduced. That has been done, I believe, by hon. members in the debate on

the motion respecting reestablishment and reconstruction. If we start a debate on social security at this stage it will I think lead to a repetition of much that has already been said in debate on the other committee. Reconstruction and reestablishment are of course not identical with social security but all three are part of a larger whole which relates to the social order-to social conditions as they exist at the present time and methods of improving them. Of the three, reconstruction and reestablishment cover a wider range and to that extent there would be the less necessity for discussing social security at any length at the moment.
I have also another reason, which is that I think members of the house generally are agreed upon the necessity of improving upon our measures of social security, increasing, enlarging and coordinating them. I do not think there is any difference of opinion among the members of the different groups in the house as to the objective to be aimed at. I believe we are all of one mind in that particular. There will inevitably be differences with respect to the means to be used to achieve those ends, but the question of the means to be adopted is a matter which is to be referred particularly to the committee and might therefore better be discussed when the committee has made its report. To start a debate at the present time might only serve to prejudice the larger objective by permitting a discussion that might develop into political controversy. I would hope that in this allimportant matter of social security this House of Commons might be able to give a lead to other representative institutions by being as nearly unanimous as possible with respect to the measures which it may feel should be put into force.
There is, of course, the further point I have mentioned at different times, the importance of not taking up too much of the time of this particular part of the session with a discussion of measures other than those that relate immediately to the all-important war measures which have to be discussed. Were it otherwise, I am sure the impression in the country would be that parliament was devoting too much of its time at this stage to post-war matters rather than to the immediate questions of the war itself.
The resolution, as hon. members will see, is an implementation of one of the undertakings set forth in the speech from the throne, the undertaking being:
. . . a comprehensive national scheme of social insurance should be worked out at once which will constitute a charter of social security for the whole of Canada.

Social Security
The government accordingly proposes to recommend the early appointment of a select committee to examine and report on the most practicable measures of social insurance, and the steps which will he required to ensure their inclusion in a national plan. Among matters which will be referred to this committee for study and consideration will be the establishment of a national system of health insurance.
I might say to hon. members that the speech from the throne in its references to social insurance and to reconstruction and reestablishment seeks to set forth the place and significance of those problems in relation to the larger question of the existing social order and the means by which that particular order may be improved. I should like to refer more particularly to the paragraphs in the speech from the throne which have this objective in view. The speech seeks to put the significance of these measures in their true light, first of all by making clear the magnitude of the question itself, and in the second place its complexity. It seeks to follow a logical sequence in setting forth the matters which have to be considered in relation to any plan of social security. Here may I point out that these social problems are first of all in the nature of world problems and that they are also all in the nature of human problems. I emphasize these two aspects because to lose sight of either is to lose sight of what is involved in trying to reach a solution of the problems themselves or how best to improve conditions.
The speech makes reference first of all to what to-day must be the first and immediate objective of any scheme which seeks to free the world from the evils of either fear or want. Obviously the first objective is to end the fear of war.
The immediate object of the united nations

I am quoting from the speech from the throne:
-is the defeat of the axis powers. Joint planning of operations on a world scale has accompanied preparations for intensive warfare. The united nations also aim at rendering aggression impossible in the future. Their governments, in addition to planning jointly for the prosecution of the war, have already entered into consultation regarding post-war problems. Achievement of their aims requires the establishment of conditions under which all peoples may enjoy equality of opportunity and a sense of security.
In other words, no solution of the question of social security can be effectively carried out so long as the axis powers continue to wage war against the free countries of the world. Until the axis powers are defeated all other tasks must necessarily be secondary.
But there is not only the task of defeating the axis powers; there is the further task of
seeing that aggression is rendered impossible in the future. Surely we have realized as the result of two world wars in the last quarter-century that all reforms may be set pretty much at naught so long as there remains the danger of aggression on the part of great powers. If aggression is to be rendered impossible in the future it is necessary that all countries join together in carrying out some policy which will make for more in the way of cooperation between the different nations and more in the way of equality of opportunity between the peoples of the different nations. It is necessary therefore that, as a background of social effort related to national purposes, there should exist a world policy which will have the effect of maintaining good and friendly relations between the many countries of the world.
When the governments of the different countries have done what lies within their power to bring about a larger measure of cooperation between nations as a whole, there will remain the problem within the individual nations themselves. It will then soon be seen that the problem of any one nation is bound up in a very close way with the position of other nations as well. If low standards of living exist in many parts of the world and high standards in a few parts, international competition, unless regulated effectively, will soon bring the high standards down to the level of the lower standards. That is why in any post-war period an effort must be made on the part of all nations that are seeking to improve their own conditions to realize that the countries of the world are members one of another, and that cooperation and mutual aid between nations will have to replace the system whereby relations between them are governed by force.
Obviously, before undertaking new measures of social security in Canada to be made applicable to all classes, our first thought must be particularly of the men who are fighting Canada's battles and the battles of freedom at the front. That is why the committee on reconstruction and reestablishment was set up at an earlier stage in this parliament than the committee on social security which is being set up at this time, and why it is proper that the committee on reconstruction and reestablishment should demand prior interest on the part of hon. members of the house. That is why in the paragraph following the one I have just read, the speech from the throne contains this statement:
Every effort must be made -to ensure, after the close of hostilities, the establishment, in
Social Security

useful and remunerative employment, of the men and women in our armed forces and in war industries. My ministers have already begun to explore the international agreements and domestic measures which will help to secure adequate incomes for primary producers and full employment after the war. With your approval, the select committee on reconstruction and reestablishment, appointed at the last session, will be reconstituted.
In. the course of the debate on the address some comment was made on the wording of that section. The question was asked, why seek adequate incomes for primary producers and full employment for the period after the war? It is apparent I think that during this war period there is a scale of employment such as has not existed in Canada at any previous time. Also, with respect to the incomes of primary producers, that they are being dealt with in several ways under the war measures of the government. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) indicated in his speech the other day the different agreements that were being entered into at this time of war which helped to ensure markets abroad for the farmers of the country and demand for their products. But what tomorrow will be seen to have been necessary above all else is that to-day we should seek to prepare the way for ensuring a continuance of markets abroad and also a continuation of full employment once the special war conditions have passed away.	[DOT]
The next paragraph is as follows:
It is in the general interest that freedom from fear and from want should be the assured possession of all. A nation-wide plan which would provide insurance against the inevitable consequences of major, economic and social hazards is essential if this objective is to be attained.
I have noticed that that paragraph has been referred to, not so much in this house but in the press of some parts of our country, as being mere platitude, that to speak of freedom from fear and from want being the assured possession of all is just talking generalities so vague as to be of no value whatever. But that is not what the clause in the speech from the throne which I have quoted really means. It sets forth what I submit is obviously in the general interest. It is the general interest that freedom from fear and from want should be the assured possession of all. That may be an ideal; it is an ideal, but it is one to be aimed at; and no one, I think, can dispute the point that if we wish to have freedom from war in the future, if we wish to have a social order whereby the men and women of our country are going to have equality of opportunity in larger measure,

the assurance of employment, and the like, then all parts of the world that are in competition with each other must also more or less be free from fear and from want.
Coming from the international aspect down to the national aspect, coming from a consideration of world conditions down to particular conditions in individual countries, the one set of hazards that is inevitable through life is, those hazards which arise out of economic and social conditions whereby individuals and families in countless numbers throughout the nation may at any time be reduced to a position, if not of destitution, at least of want, and certainly be held continuously in fear alike of both destitution and want. There are certain hazards which do exist under the industrial organization of society as it has come to be in our time, and which exists not through any fault of employers, not through any fault of employees, but simply from the condition in which organized society finds itself at the present time. There may be in a highly industrial organized state such as ours is, a situation where a financial crisis in another country may bring about industrial depression over a long period in our own. We all know how that fact has been verified by experience between the period of the last war and the present time. It cannot be put down to the fault of employers or of employees that thousands of men and women in our country are thrown out of work in periods of depression, when the depression arises not from conditions as they exist in our particular country but from conditions as they exist in other parts of the world. For many years past it has been recognized that a cotton famine for example in the southern United States can throw large numbers of workers out of work in the cotton textile industries in Britain. That Is but an example of what in our day takes place in all parts of the world at all times. The competition of foreign labour, some new invention, high tariffs suddenly imposed, all these and many other things may affect the lives of countless men and women and leave them in a position not only of fear but very soon in a position of want and destitution.
Society having created-I put it in that particular way-conditions which permit of that sort of thing, society has to find some way to remedy it. I use the word "society" instead of "the state" because I want it to be seen that what I am saying relates to the social organization of human beings in the different countries of the globe, under an industrial system such as we have to-day. What social insurance seeks to do is to find a means whereby these inevitable hazards will be met

Social Security
in some part at least through the action of the state and through action prescribed by the state.
These hazards are well known. The most common of course is unemployment. Other hazards are those arising out of old age, blindness, sickness and invalidity, the death of the breadwinner, birth and burial, where the funds to meet the obligations that arise out of these cannot be provided for in advance. Unemployment may come at any time, on a small or large scale, through no fault of their own on the part of those affected.
Any constructive system of social security is based on the theory that all industry is, or ought to be, in the nature of social service; that industry is not merely a means whereby capitalists may increase profits, or workers find the means of gaining a livelihood through wages; but that there exists also the right of the community, which makes possible the carrying on of industry, to expect that the interests and well-being of the community and its members will also be considered in the rewards of industry. In other words, industry exists to serve a social end, as well as to serve the needs of individuals. Under that view men and women are the great asset of the state. The well-being of all the human resources, the men and women, who supply the labour, the thought and skill essential for planning and carrying on industry ought to be the first concern of the state. And where the state makes possible the carrying on of industry, they are entitled to have the state see that they are protected against inevitable hazards.
May I pause to say a word as to the part the state plays in permitting industry to be carried on. Have in mind any of the large manufacturing industries, and ask ourselves the question: could these industries be carried on at all except for what organized society in the state does to make their existence possible? In the first place the state maintains law and order, without which no industry could exist for any length of time. Law and order are maintained at the expense of the taxpayers of the community. The state makes possible trade and the maintenance of foreign markets through its diplomatic and consular services, its subsidies to transportation companies, through the permission it gives transportation companies to construct their ways across the territory of the nation. The state controls inventions and patents. One could go on indicating many things to show that the carrying on of industry is made possible through the fact that the state is organized as we know it to be.
But above and beyond all that, the material resources of a country exist within the confines of the country and it is only by the implied expressed permission of the state that the institution of private property can exist. The justification of private property lies in the fact that it has been thought that because of what private property ensures' of initiative, self reliance and the like, the good of the greatest number will thereby best be served. But if as a result of the institution of private property, whether it be the ownership of land or of capital, a social condition may develop which is inimical to the community as a whole, that institution has either to be modified in some particulars, controlled in some directions, or make way for some other system.
Social security does not seek necessarily, or, at all, in some cases, to abolish the institution of private property. It seeks rather to ensure that the benefits of private property will be secured to the community at large, and that through an inequitable distribution of wealth the institution of private property shall not be made a means whereby a very few may become increasingly rich and a great many suffer because of the inequalities that exist. Everywhere there are vast inequalities of circumstances and of opportunities. There is no doubt that society as it is organized to-day does enable those who are economically strong to become stronger, and at the same time does have the effect of causing the economically weak in many of the great struggles of life to become weaker while the wealth of the world has vastly increased, its distribution has become increasingly disproportionate. Community considerations afford opportunities to some, and impose handicaps on others. We -see everywhere evidences of the fact that those that have large abundance find it possible to survive all the existing hazards, find it possible to go on increasing their wrealth; while those who possess very little of this world's goods are the first to go completely to the wall when a condition arises such as has arisen from time to time through depressions and extensive unemployment.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON NATIONAL SOCIAL INSURANCE
speechtext: That is because they did not save when they had the opportunity!

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON NATIONAL SOCIAL INSURANCE
speechtext:
As my hon. friend is aware, all depends on how much chance there is to save. Great care has to be taken in any scheme of social insurance not to discourage saving, and I think social insurance plans will have that carefully in view. But I wish to re-emphasize that in the order of things as they are to-day emphasis is put in very large part upon position rather than on human personality; is put upon wealth rather
Social Security

than upon life; and that under any scheme of social security it is life and personality which it is intended should be the first consideration of the state and of those who are exercising authority in the carrying on of its affairs. Industrial policy must be founded upon recognition of human personality and upon recognition of community well-being.
I should like now to say a word as to the procedure set forth in the resolution. It is suggested that a committee should be appointed to consider the whole question of social security and to consider it in different aspects. Some one may repeat, as has already been said I think in the course of the debate on the address, that the government should not have to -have a committee to advise, or rather to give it a policy; that the government ought to have a policy of its own. Well, the government has a policy, a very definite policy, which is set forth in the speech from the throne, and which I have already read. The government's policy is to bring into being a comprehensive national scheme of social insurance.
Why has the government deemed a reference of the matter to a select committee the most essential first step in seeking to deal with so large a measure of social security? The reason is that already in Canada we have a large number of social security measures which have grown up in a more or less haphazard manner. They have to be correlated and coordinated in one plan if progress is to be made on a national scale. They have not been introduced one in relation to the other; they have not been introduced in the one assembly. They have been introduced at one time in this parliament, at other times in provincial parliaments, but they have never been coordinated into one scheme. It is obvious that where there are social measures of that character, each having the same objective, unless they are correlated there is bound to be a great deal of overlapping and a great deal of additional cost in administration, and certain to be a great deal of confusion. It would seem, therefore, that the first step in moving further in the direction of social security would be to study carefully the existing measures of our own country and then study carefully the existing measures in other countries and the proposals that have been put forth by those who have given special study to the question of social security.
Had it wished to do so the government might have appointed a royal commission to undertake this task of surveying conditions here and presenting a national scheme. It might have called in experts and been advised by them, but it was felt that this, together
	.
with reconstruction and reestablishment, is the largest question the country is likely to have before it for our generation, and that it would be in the public interest, and particularly in the interests of members of parliament themselves, that they should have an opportunity of familiarizing themselves with the various factors bearing on this allimportant question. And it was felt that this could be best effected by having a select committee of the house to study the whole matter. I should think it would be advisable for this committee to retain experts. Speaking for the government I may say that it will afford whatever in the way of facilities for effective study and research the committee itself may deem necessary and essential.
The resolution suggests that there should be subcommittees as well as the one main committee; that is because of the extent of the study that will have to be made. It will be noticed that special reference is made to health insurance. It was felt there was need to make perfectly clear some aspects of social security which perhaps were deserving of more immediate consideration than some other aspects. It has seemed to the government that the question of health insurance was in that position. That is so for this reason, that already we have on our statute book a plan of unemployment insurance and a system of old age pensions, both established by the federal parliament; we have a system of government annuities, also established by the federal parliament; we have pensions to veterans, pensions to the blind and other forms of pensions, also established by this federal government. Then in the provinces they have a series of different social measures, some of them related to accidents and others to sickness, hospitalization, widows' and mothers' allowances, maternity benefits and so on, all of which are in the nature of social security measures but which differ greatly as between the several provinces. They are not correlated in one great national scheme, and if Canada is to make progress in this field the first step now is to have the whole field surveyed and in some way as far as may be possible, a national scheme outlined.
In stating to the British people what he had found necessary in the way of study for his report Sir William Beveridge said he had been closely following all social legislation for a period of something like thirty years. Happily the committee will have the benefit of the thirty years' experience of Sir William Beveridge. I mention this simply because Sir William felt it necessary to draw the attention

Social Security
of the British people to the careful study he had given the question before making his report.
I wish to draw attention to an attitude toward social security measures that has been taken in some quarters since the government's policy was announced in the speech from the throne. When the Atlantic charter was proclaimed it met with universal acceptance in this country. I have yet to find a newspaper in Canada which had not a good word to say for the Atlantic charter. One of the things most prominently proclaimed in connection with the Atlantic charter was the fact that among other things it did aim to bring about an increased measure of social security in the post-war period. I have been looking at the journals of this country, and I find that to-day some are inclined to belittle, at least, the idea of social security, as being something vague and general, something that will involve outlays greater than any country may be able to meet. Sir William Beveridge has said that he regarded social insurance as the first step to be taken toward meeting the main objectives of the Atlantic charter in so far as it had to do with social conditions. It is, I think, from that point of view that we should view questions that relate to social security.
The committee has been asked not only to give the study which I have suggested, but to report to the house on the most practicable measures of social insurance, the steps which will be required to ensure their inclusion in a national plan. Let it not be said that the committee is simply to make a study and do nothing else. If this resolution carries, the committee will have a very definite instruction from this house to do something positive, as set out in these words: to report on the most practicable measures of social insurance and the steps which will be required to ensure their inclusion in a national plan. I need not emphasize the importance of what will be involved in effecting that particular end. There are questions of finance that will have to be very carefully considered. It is not going to help any scheme of social insurance for the government to bring forward a measure that in the end may not prove practicable. So that what may be possible will have to be studied in relation to the obligations that already exist in several directions and what it is felt can be carried on in conjunction with other obligations.
Questions of jurisdiction will arise, questions between the provinces and the dominion as to whether in a national scheme the dominion should attempt to carry out all social
security measures, or whether those measures in part should be under the jurisdiction of the dominion and in part under that of the several provinces. So far as administration is concerned there are some measures which, at least for a time, the provinces will I believe wish to retain. There may be others they will be prepared to hand over to the federal government.
Then there will arise immediately the question as to the source from which revenue is to be derived to carry out the different measures. That is something which will require careful consideration. The purpose of the government in this whole matter is, as quickly as may be possible, to reach an immediate improvement in and enlargement of social security measures in our country. But we realize that that cannot be done effectively until the whole position or field receives careful study.
The only other feature I might mention is the size of the committee. It is a large committee, consisting of forty-one members, to be exact. That, again, has been thought advisable for the reasons I have already indicated. So long as those of us who are in this chamber to-day continue to have any part in public affairs we shall find, as a main interest in our lives and in the life of our country, this problem of social security. The more hon. members can familiarize themselves in an intimate way with this question in all its bearings, the better it will be not only for hon. members themselves in rendering the kind of service they would hope to render to the state, but the better it will also be for the state itself. Members of this parliament have an exceptional opportunity to render a great service to their own and future generations.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON NATIONAL SOCIAL INSURANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in attempting to
speak in connection with the setting up and constitution of this important committee, one which will deal with the whole subject of social insurance and social security, I should like to say that with some parts of the Prime Minister's (Mr. Mackenzie King) address I am in agreement.
The House of Commons must realize that the winning of the war is the first, the major consideration of our deliberations. We must not at any time allow any other issues to interfere with our winning of the war, nor must we permit other considerations to come first. But inextricably woven into our whole war effort is the undeniable fact that there are scores of thousands, yes, hundreds of thousands of men and women who to-day, both overseas and in Canada, are fighting our

Social Security

battle of freedom, and who are anxious to know that while they are fighting and are indicating their willingness to give life and limb we, here, shall be doing something to prepare for that better world for which they fight.
As far as social security and our whole scheme for a better world order are concerned, it seems to me it is not possible entirely to separate our plans for peace from our actual movements in the field of war itself. I believe almost every hon. member who has talked to younger men enlisted in his majesty's forces must have heard a statement which, on many occasions, I have heard. They must have heard it from our war workers, and the challenge it presents cannot be escaped. During the years of depression through which every nation in the world had the misfortune to pass, during those terrible years of privation and suffering with which, for some reason or another our society and our system were not able to cope successfully; during those years when we were not able to operate with full employment for our people, certain thoughts developed in the minds of our people. The result is that to-day our young men-yes, and young women, too-are considering this thought: When it comes to a war of destruction, we find the money to fight it, but when a few years ago we were faced with a war for better conditions for our people somehow or another we were not able to put our people to work. And that, let us remember, was a condition which was not confined to any one country, but was found in every nation. Perhaps at times this thought is exaggerated, and some may think too great emphasis is placed upon it; but it is a view which parliament must not lightly toss aside.
The House of Commons cannot overlook this challenge. It is a challenge to which we must give every consideration because, linked with our whole problem of social security and post-war conditions, is the thought that somehow, by some system, we must find jobs, work and wages for our people. That is the first objective toward which we must move.
There are different views as to how this can best be accomplished. Perhaps none of us in these changing days can be so dogmatic as to say that our solution-and I believe each individual has one; certainly almost every hon. member seems to have one-without the help of others will solve the problem. But the pooling of the best thought, thought which reflects the anxious minds and the most sincere desires of our people, will in my opinion eventually solve our problem and meet the challenge.

May I point out; however, that there is a feeling throughout Canada, one which will show itself in any movements which lie ahead, that when the war is over we shall have a higher sense of human values and shall give lesser emphasis to material things than we have done heretofore. If we fail in this it is my belief that we shall not win the peace for which we have longed in these years of war. The days of reaction have gone and I hope they have gone for keeps. There is no room for reactionary ideas in a w'orld that is moving perhaps more quickly than most of us realize.
In keeping abreast of that moving world, let us not forget that we as members of this parliament must take our stand in the forefront of aggressive and progressive reform. Not only must we keep abreast; we must give leadership to that movement. In connection with this further post-Winnipeg reform which the Prime Minister brought down in the speech from the throne I should like to congratulate him upon being perhaps a converted reader of the programme and the policy laid down by the Progressive Conservative party on that occasion. .
