speechtext: You got the idea from the Prime Minister and you should thank him for it, not congratulate him.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON NATIONAL SOCIAL INSURANCE
speechtext:
I only wanted to congratulate the Prime Minister; I hope the hon. member for Brantford City will not think I am doing anything other than that. I wish to say that in so far as our programme is concerned, it was a result which came from a great movement emanating from all parts of this dominion and leading toward a reformation of our economic and social structure.
Referring to the remarks made by the Prime Minister in connection with this motion I should like to point out to him that it will not be enough for the people of Canada simply to have the government set out in a speech from the throne the objectives to which they are moving. We all know the objectives to which they are moving, or toward which they should move, but we are entitled to more than that in a speech from the throne; we are entitled to be told the policy of this government. With great deference to the Prime Minister I must say that I do not think he made a very good job this afternoon of explaining the difference between the objectives of his party and the policy which the government of that party adopts. I hope in all earnestness that the report of this committee will not be brought down so close to the end of the session that there will not be time to bring in legislation

Social Security
which may be founded upon the recommendations of the committee. Canada will not be satisfied with just a report of a committee with respect to the whole matter of social security. Canada will be satisfied only with, first, the bringing down of a report by the committee and then the introduction of legislation dealing with the recommendations contained in the report.
As far as health insurance is concerned, it seems to me that we should have had the health insurance bill in this house before any such legislation is considered by the social security committee. That is not going to be done, and I do not intend to deal further with that at the moment. Our unemployment insurance law forms one of the great parts of our social security scheme, but there are many things still to be desired with respect to that law. I point this out in order that this committee may consider how we can improve the whole system of unemployment insurance.
One question is being asked by the working people of this country, and it should be answered. I am sure this question is being asked of other hon. members who must have the support of labour to retain their seats. The labouring mail likes the principle of the act, and we all have endorsed that principle. Here is what he is saying: If I am fired I do not get the benefits; if I quit I do not get the benefits; if I am sick I do not get the benefits-when do I get the benefits?- Of course the answer is obvious, but on the other hand I think the committee should consider this particular aspect of unemployment insurance.
There was a point I raised in the unemployment insurance committee which I raise, again. I do not think any act can be perfect, but it is our job to make these acts as perfect as human brains can make them. Our working men should be assured that when they are out of employment, when they are ill or incapacitated, some benefits will be made available to them. This is what the working man is asking for to-day, and I think it is one of the subjects that should be dealt with by the committee.
When the report of the unemployment insurance committee was brought down it was pointed out that this legislation was only a- step toward an objective, and the house was cautioned at the time not to expect too much from the Unemployment Insurance Act. Up to the present we have not needed the benefits available under this act to the extent that perhaps the act contemplated, but at the best it can constitute only a token 72537-60}
piece of security for the working man and his family. We must do better than that for him.
When a working man becomes sick and loses his job there is no machinery under the Unemployment Insurance Act to provide him with benefits because he cannot meet the test of availability for employment. Where is his security? That man may be anywhere between the ages of forty and seventy years, and he must depend largely upon the charity of his friends or those who will come to his rescue. This is another matter that should be considered by the committee.
I was interested in what the Prime Minister said about not having forgotten the old virtues of thrift and saving. We must not forget those. The character of the people of this country is such that they are imbued with the idea of saving for a rainy day. However, there are many people who through no fault of their own are not able to provide the necessary umbrella for the rainy day of sickness and old age and incapacity. I refer more particularly to the necessity for improvement in our old age pension scheme. In Canada we adopted the principle of old age pensions, and I find that throughout the dominion there is very little criticism of that principle. It is a principle which the people of Canada believe in, that of securing to our older people a better deal for their old age, and once having adopted that principle we must carry it out in practice in such a way as to meet the conditions under which our older people find themselves from time to time. I am hopeful that the committee in dealing with old age pensions will first of all consider a reduction in the present age limit. There are many reasons for that, but I emphasize it largely on account of our experience since the act first came into operation. People for one reason or another seem to be burning out at an earlier age. Perhaps it is the speed at which our modern life is conducted. It seems to me that the -age of seventy is now outworn as the standard age for granting the old Tige pension, and I should like to see the committee give serious consideration to reducing the present age limit.
Furthermore, I should like to see the committee do something else which is almost just as important as reducing the age limit. I should like them to give consideration to the many increases that have taken place in the cost of living and to readjust the amount of the old age pension so that our older people will feel that their security has been protected as not only in principle but also in actual practice as far as parliament is concerned.
Social Security

I do not want to labour the point, but I believe that our older people in Canada also deserve a word of encouragement from this parliament. These men and women through the years have borne the burden and heat of the day and the toil of the years. We owe them a great deal more than sometimes we are prone to admit. I should like to see these men and women in the evening of their life not subjected to the petty investigations that are sometimes made by all kinds of organizations, governmental if you like, and carried to the point where many of our older people are almost afraid to apply for an old age pension because of the many inquiries that are made into their circumstances from time to time. I should like the committee to give serious consideration to this whole question of the means test for old age pensioners and to the question of what I fear are sometimes unnecessary petty investigations into their circumstances generally.
Another matter correlated to old age pensions is pensions for the blind. I remember well when Mr. Dunning, then Minister of Finance, brought in his bill for pensions for the blind in one of the years following 1936. The House of Commons on that occasion lived up to its highest traditions in endorsing unanimously this measure for relieving the sufferings of those who had become incapacitated through blindness. It appealed not only to the minds but to the hearts of hon. members. But there again an age limit was fixed for pensions for the blind. I hope that the committee will give serious consideration to reducing that age limit. There may have to be some age limit, but it seems to me that a man who, at thirty years of age, is incapacitated by blindness from earning a living is in the same position, as far as incapacity goes, as a man who is incapacitated by blindness at forty.
But blindness is only one form of incapacity. I should like to see the committee make a special effort to bring into our great social security scheme another group of men and women in Canada who are too often forgotten by governments and by our people generally. I refer to those men and women who for other reasons than blindness, it may be paralysis or other causes into which I could go in greater detail had I the time, are wholly incapacitated from earning a living and unable to take their place in the social and economic world of to-day. Let us not as a nation overlook those men and women. Their plight has been brought before the house on a previous occasion, and I am bringing it before the house again to-day in . the hope that the committee which will deal with the

whole broad matter of social security will not forget the plight of those men and women because, if we are subscribing to the new order as we should be doing, we must never forget that the new order comprises a great many classes and that this is one of them.
May I say a word on health insurance. The Minister of Pensions and1 National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) is prone, as are other members of the government, to refer from time to time to a draft bill as a memorandum. In dealing with the question of health insurance the minister called the draft bill on health insurance a memorandum. The minister is not in his seat at the moment; otherwise I might pursue the matter further. Suffice it to say that the rumour has been rife throughout Canada that for a considerable time there has been in the minister's department a draft bill or several draft bills on health insurance. After the many consultations there have been with men who have made a study of this subject, I believe this country expected that the Minister of Pensions and National Health would have brought down legislation on the subject at the beginning of this session. Instead, however, we find that a different policy has been adopted, whereby this and the other matters in the social security programme have been lumped together to be dealt with by the social security committee. I fail to see why the government did not bring down health insurance legislation at once. When it had been dealt with by the house and had gone through its various stages here it could1 if necessary, have been remitted to the social security committee, but I think this house ought to have had legislation on health insurance brought down before it had to run the gamut of the social security committee. The reasons for this, in my opinion, are fairly obvious. As far as I know, all the other matters which will be dealt with by the social security committee are the subjects of acts which are already on the statute books of the provinces or the dominion. But with regard to health insurance, although it will constitute probably the most important and far-reaching of all the enactments to be dealt with by the committee, a bill has not been brought down to the house. That angle should not be overlooked, and I draw it to the attention of the government.
The problem of health insurance is an appalling one for the citizens of Canada. .It is also one which will not be entirely devoid of danger; and I think that, since the committee is to deal with it before legislation is brought in, any standardized or dominionwide scheme should give special attention and the most exacting care to the problems of

Social Security
localities-municipalities and the lesser units of our dominion legislative jurisdiction-so that when the health insurance measure comes in, it will be found to be workable having regard to the various localities in which it will have to operate. In this country we have wide divergencies, occupational, geographical, and other, among our people. For that reason care must be exercised in the general scheme so that our health insurance act shall have sufficient elasticity to be workable. Anything less will not meet the situation.
Throughout Canada there is an insistent demand for action on this matter. For many years we have had this spectre in our midst Men who do not make a lot of money, people in the low income brackets, have a fear not only of unemployment but of the ravages, dangers and cost of sickness and ill health. Who among us has not had that fear from time to time? One may be able- some are-to prepare for the day when he is out of work; he may provide for many other eventualities and contingencies. But the great fear which haunts many people and has haunted them for a long time, particularly those who are not able to put away much for a rainy day, is the apprehension that they or their families will be subject to a long and serious illness and that they will not be able to meet the doctors', nurses', hospital and other medical bills which accumulate by virtue thereof. How many people within our own knowledge have been financially ruined almost for life through that very condition? Therefore, it seems to me, this health measure is probably long overdue, and this government and this parliament, if they can do something to alleviate the existing conditions and assure our people in the lower income brackets of some freedom from fears of sickness and of long periods of unemployment as a result of such conditions, will do something for the country in general which will be thoroughly worth while.
I hope that when a general health scheme is embodied in the form of legislation we shall not forget that some emphasis, perhaps the major emphasis, should be placed upon preventive medicine. An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. Those simple words, which have been used many times during the last scores of years, contain as important a truth and carry as much weight as they ever did. The health of our people is one of the most valuable of our national assets, and in preserving it we not only avoid sickness but escape the additional cost which inevitably follows if earlier preventive, steps
have not been taken. As far as is humanly possible we should have social conditions in which every child and adult will be able to develop a sound mind and a sound body. I know this is not fully possible, but it ought to be one of our objectives, one to which the committee should give its constant, energetic and earnest attention. Health must be no longer regarded as a wholly private responsibility. Being, as it is, essential to our national development, there must be public responsibility as well. In this regard I say to the minister in charge of the committee that we shall expect legislation which will meet with the approval of the people and will prove workable from the point of view which, we are endeavouring to attain.
In connection with the social security committee I would say this to the Prime Minister. He mentioned bringing experts in to guide and advise the committee in its work. Probably that will be necessary. Perhaps, when he speaks of having in mind a comparison of schemes of social security in other parts of the world, he is thinking of bringing to Canada authorities from elsewhere who can give advice on that point. But in the newspapers last week there appeared this rather interesting item, dated from London on February 25. It said:
Sir William Beveridge, whose recent "cradle-to-the-grave" social security plan created a wide rift of opinion in parliament, will visit the United States and perhaps Canada on a non-government mission, he disclosed to-day.
He revealed he intends to make a private survey of the causes and remedies for unemployment.
I suggest that the government should, if it has not already done so, avail itself of the services and the advice of Sir William Beveridge. If he is in this part of the continent and can find it convenient to attend a meeting of the committee, I suggest that he be invited to give his advice with respect to the problem which he has been studying in the old land. I realize that the Beveridge report can be only a guide in a certain way with regard to our problems here. On the other hand it may well be, as I think the Prime Minister or someone else pointed out in the debate on the address, that conditions in the old land and conditions here are not entirely comparable. Whether or not that is the situation, the general principles for which both countries are working and the objectives at which they are aiming make it important that if possible this committee should have the benefit of the advice of one who has made a study not merely of the British system, and has been responsible for this much talked of report, and that he should be available as far as our

Social Security
committee is concerned. Therefore, in closing, I wish to indicate to the Prime Minister, in case he has not given as Close study to it as the speech from the throne would rather indicate he had, the stand of the Progressive Conservative party with respect to one or two items in connection with our whole social security programme which I think are of importance at this time. This is what is said in that platform:
A social security programme, the adoption of which we advocate, would include in a unified system:
(a)	Unemployment insurance;
(b)	Adequate payments for the maintenance of unemployables;
(c)	Retirement insurance.
To which I should like to see the committee give serious consideration.
(d)	The payment of increased old age pensions, at a reduced age, until such time as the retirement insurance scheme becomes fully operative;
(e)	Adequate pensions for the blind;
(f)	Adequate mothers' and widows' allowance.
This in general sums up the feeling of those many men and women who attended that great convention:
We recognize the obligation of government to make available to every citizen adequate medical, dental, nursing, hospital and pre-natal care, and to further advance public health and nutritional principles so that health may be safeguarded and preserved. This programme is to be financed under a contributory system supplemented by government assistance.
May I close with these words: The adoption of a widespread and comprehensive system of social security in Canada will to my way of thinking be a definite step toward the objective of a new world order and a new order for the Canadian people jointly. It has been well pointed out that at this stage of international affairs we cannot, with respect to our own domestic problems, rely entirely upon what other nations do. One of the best jobs we can do in putting the whole world in order is to see to it that our own house is put in order, as well as the others. I do not think our job is first of all to put everyone's house in order, nor do I think it is our job to have everyone come here and put our house in order. The best job we can do, at least in a preliminary way, is to see to it that our house in Canada is put in such shape that we can fit into a broad international picture which will ensure peace, good-will and the brotherhood of man in the years that lie ahead.

speakeroldname: Mr. S. H. KNOWLES (Winnipeg North Centre):
maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON NATIONAL SOCIAL INSURANCE
speechtext:
I rise to speak on this motion because of its great importance, and because I feel that 
the people whom I have the honour to represent would want me to take part in this debate. I say that despite the admonition given to us a short time ago by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to curtail if possible this discussion. As a new member in this house I confess I have been disturbed by the frequency with which it is suggested to private members that discussion should be boiled down to a minimum. That is not my conception of my duty as a member of this house, particularly when an important matter such as this is before us; and in view of the fact that some of us are not on the committee I feel it is our duty to make our contribution to the work of this committee when it is being set up.
The motion that is before us arises out of a deep conviction on the part of a great majority of our Canadian people, and indeed of the people of all the united nations, that the time has come to rid this world not only of fascism but also of want and of fear. That our people want us to do this is beyond all argument. Our job is to get down to brass tacks and do something about it.
Another point about which there should be no argument is that social insurance is one means of defence against want and fear. In a moment or two I want to emphasize the fact that because social insurance is a second line of defence we must pay some attention to the front line as well. But first of all I want to make perfectly clear the attitude of this group towards the Prime Minister's motion. It calls for the setting up of a select committee "to examine and report on a national plan of social insurance". To propose anything less at this stage of our history would be unthinkable. We shall support the motion. But we urge the government to go further and to bring down during this session legislation that will provide for the immediate establishment in Canada of social security at least to the extent that is now being enjoyed in our sister dominion of New Zealand, as it was so well outlined in Ottawa last May by Hon. Walter Nash.
I shall not dwell on the political consequences of failure on the part of the present government to bring down such legislation without delay; that can be left to the electorate. But I should like to emphasize the fact-I know it has been said time and again in this house, but it can be underlined- that our people are putting everything they have into the present conflict. Its cost in human life, in sacrifice, in all kinds of changes in our standards and ways of life, is immeasurable. If after this conflict is over, after all these sacrifices, we find ourselves with no adequate defences against want and fear, this

Social Security
government if it has failed to provide those defences will have betrayed the people of Canada in a most critical period of their history, and in particular they will have betrayed those in our armed forces. To say at that time that back in 1943 a select committee was set up will not suffice. The government must face its responsibility to introduce legislation now. Pious language about a " charter of social security for the whole of Canada " will not do. It is not good enough for lion, members opposite to say, as many said in the course of the debate on setting up the committee on reconstruction and reestablishment, that they agree with many of our ideas for post-war security. The Liberal party is in power now. It is its responsibility, not to tell us what it will do five or ten years hence, but to bring down legislation now that will protect the people of this country against want and fear in the post-war world.
Now, Mr. Speaker, without lessening in any way my insistence that the government should bring down legislation during this session along the lines I have suggested, I want to urge upon the house a realization of the fact that social insurance at best is only a second line of defence against economic hazards, and that in the long run it will fail unless it is established in its proper place in our economy. I refer again to the statements along this line made by Sir William Beveridge in his report. At page 6 he says:
Organization of social insurance should be treated as one part only of a comprehensive policy of social progress.
Earlier on the same page he makes this significant statement:
A revolutionary moment in the world's history is a time for revolutions, not for patching.
On page 163 Sir William Beveridge makes some statements which have been made in this house already but which I feel warrant repetition. He is discussing, as a necessary condition to the workability of his own plans, the necessity of maintaining employment. He gives five reasons for his contention, of which I am going to quote the last two:
Fourth, and most important, income security which is all that can be given by social insurance is so inadequate a provision for human happiness that to put it forward by itself as a sole or principal measure of reconstruction hardly seems worth doing. It should be accompanied by an announced determination to use the powers of the state to whatever extent may prove necessary to ensure for all, not indeed absolute continuity of work, but a reasonable chance of productive employment.
Fifth, though it should be within the power of the community to bear the cost of the whole plan for social security, the cost is heavy and,
if to the necessary cost waste is added, it may become insupportable. Unemployment, both through increasing expenditure on benefit and through reducing the income to bear those costs, is the worst form of waste.
So, Mr. Speaker, I wish to emphasize that the first and all-important line of defence against the hazards with which we are concerned is the ordering of our economy so that it will provide employment for all, together with the production of the goods and services necessary to provide a high standard of living, and the distribution of those goods among our people according to need. As I understand it, the purpose of social insurance, and of certain forms of social security which are on other than an insurance basis, is to provide protection when and where the economic system fails. But if the economic system is so full of contradictions that it is certain to break down time and again, resulting in mass unemployment with all of its hazards, it is impossible to devise a scheme of social insurance that will protect our people.
With reference to health insurance I should like to point out that if our economic system condemns millions of our people to malnutrition, to living in slums and substandard houses, in city and country alike, it is economically impossible to work out a health insurance scheme that will take care of the ill health of our people under those conditions. So that if we in this house mean what we say when we set out to devise a "charter of social security for the whole of Canada," I insist that we must give our attention to the setting up of an economic order in which social security can be maintained and in which so-called social insurance schemes will work. Social security will be a fact only when the total economy is one of security. Social insurance will work over a long period of time only when the need for its benefits is incidental and not wholesale. This means, as I see it, that our primary task is to establish an economic order which will make possible the production of an abundance of goods and services, which will distribute the nation's necessary work among our people according to ability and capacity, and which in turn will distribute the abundance that we produce amongst our people according to need. It is true that even in that kind of economy there will be certain cases of need, and properly speaking that is where social insurance should come in; those are the conditions under which social insurance can be expected to work. In other words, when social insurance functions as it should, as a second line of defence against want and fear, it can be set up in such a way

speechtext:
If that transcends the rules of the house, I will withdraw the statement. Nevertheless the statement is made in many quarters that any programme such as we are suggesting costs money, and because it will cost money it cannot be considered, particularly in view of the large amount we are spending just now. It is said that our war programme will leave us brankrupt at the end of the war. I am sure the Minister of Finance will agree with me when I say that such a statement is sheer nonsense, and that after all the spending of money even on the scale we are proposing to spend it during the forthcoming fiscal year is only an index.
The reality of the present situation is that we have increased our production tremendously, and that we are waging war out of our current production. Similarly we can build a million new homes after the war ends, and we can feed and clothe our people, out of our then current production, if only we will produce according to our capacity, and not within absurd financial and profitmaking limitations. If we try to go back to the old order of unrestricted exploitation, the best we can look for from any form of social insurance set up within such an order is the "rationed poverty" which has been mentioned of late by certain political leaders in the country. But I insist we of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation are right in maintaining that neither "rationed poverty" nor "pockets of unemployment" are good enough for the people of Canada in the post-war world. If we can produce materials to the value of nine billions of dollars a year, while the war is on, we can do likewise, in peace time, and thus provide a good life for our people.
I wish to say further in connection with this matter of cost that sometimes we who hold the views I am presenting are accused of wanting the people of Canada, and particularly the farmers and the workers for whom we speak, to be given something for nothing. This charge is levelled at us particularly when we ask for certain social services and benefits such as a larger old-age pension at an earlier age, adequate provision for war veterans, and for widows of war veterans; for a national plan for the care of our health, including preventive measures, and for a national housing programme. Let me make it clear that in our view none of these things can be had for nothing. We are not asking that they be provided out of thin air. These things call for expenditures. They cost. But, Mr. Speaker, what is it that they cost? They cost the human effort of our people, applied to raw materials. Our workers, farmers and fishermen, including our scientists, technicians and white-collar workers of all kinds, in their daily toil, are paying the real cost of our present national production, so far as human beings are concerned.
I say again that our nine-billion-dollar level of national production has been achieved because the necessary expenditure of human effort is being made by the citizens of our country. What we ask is that this volume of production, the cost of, which is being met by the labour and toil of our people, be distributed among our people according to equity and need. At the present time a large portion of our national production, which represents an expenditure of effort on the part of our people, is being applied as our people want it applied, namely, in their interest, in the defence of our country, and of freedom itself. All right; we ask that when peace comes the same principle be carried out, and that a similarly large portion of our national production, the cost of which our people as a whole will gladly pay through their daily toil on the farm, in the factory, in the office, in the schoolroom and laboratory, be channelled into the things that will provide security and a good life for all our people.
Someone asks where a million new houses will come from. They will come out of our then current production in the same way that our vast war supplies are coming out of to-day's current production. When we ask for old age pensions of at least $30 a month- and I see no reason why the figure should not be $40 or $50 a month-starting at the age of sixty-five, or even younger, someone will want to know where the money will come from. It will come out of our then current' production in the same way that we are maintaining our armed forces, 700,000 strong, out of today's current production.
We ask that the men and women in our armed forces be kept on regular pay and allowances until they are adequately reestablished after the war, and that medical care be
Social Security

made available to them for life, thus avoiding the difficulties in this connection encountered by the veterans of the last war. The question then arises in some quarters, where will the money come from? It will come out of our then current production, just as we are providing pay and allowances and medical care out of to-day's current production.
All of this will depend upon our maintaining our present volume of production, which I understand is nine billions of dollars to-day. Ten years ago I believe it was less than three billions of dollars. If we have any intention of going back to unrestricted exploitation which produces only for the sake of profit; if we have any intention of going back to an annual production of five, four, or three billions of dollars, then there will not be the slightest chance of any social insurance scheme that we may devise being of any value.
Social security calls first and foremost for the maintenance of a high level of production and for the distribution of that production, or shall I say the channelling of it into the things that will provide a good life for all our people. This good life, as I see it, should include other things, but at least it must include homes to live in, adequate food and clothing, care of health and a fair measure of life'* luxuries for everyone, with dignified security in old age. Nothing less than such a programme is good enough for the Canadian people when the war is over.
I was interested in some of the comments made to-day by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), and I endeavoured to jot down one sentence in particular with which I thoroughly agreed. I believe Hansard will bear out the sense of what I have jotted down. He said that no country goes bankrupt by increasing its production and devoting a large portion of that production to a supreme cause. We are doing that to-day, to the supreme cause of the present struggle. We ask that the same thing be done to-morrow, to the supreme cause of establishing and making possible a good life for the Canadian people.
There was a day when the vested interests through their newspapers and in other ways could treat the farmers and workers of this country a though they were a class apart, as though they should be grateful for the crumbs given to them from Canada's economic table. That situation does not hold any longer. Our young men for whom a few years ago there was no place in our life are to-day in positions of defence vital to our national existence and freedom. I sometimes think when I see these young men going away with "Canada" on their shoulders that in a very

real sense they are Canada. They are full participants in the great struggle in which we are engaged. When these young men come back it is not going to be possible to shove them out into the cold to wait until something comes along. They are participants in this great struggle, and they deserve to be full participants in our economic life after the war is over. That means that they deserve to have jobs and to receive income sufficient to make it possible for them to share in the wealth which we hope they will be producing.
I sometimes wonder if hon. members have realized the change that has taken place in the thinking of our people. During the course of this war we have had to learn to pool our resources and work together, to think in terms of the larger community of which we are a part. That has been true both on the home front and on the battlefront. The result is that our people expect that after the war they will all be able to participate in whatever life it is possible to establish in this country. As I see it, that is what the people look for now when they envision social security.
There might have been a day twenty or thirty years ago when unemployment insurance, the providing of a few incidental benefits and a few dollars a week, would have been acceptable as social security. But that day is gone. As the previous speaker, the leader of the opposition, pointed out, our people to-day agree with the principle of unemployment insurance, but when you tell them that this legislation will provide only a few dollars a week under certain conditions, that to them is not social security. It may have been a form of social security twenty or thirty years ago, but to-day social security involves the establishment of a national economy of a high order, full production, and the provision that everyone who is willing and capable of working shall share in that production. Those who through no fault of their own are not able to share in the work are entitled, as human beings in a civilized society, to share in the goods and services that are produced. Social security is much more than the incidental schemes the government has suggested. I feel it is even more than the comprehensive scheme of social insurance to which the immediately preceding speaker referred. It calls for comprehensive changes in the whole nature of our economy, and that is what we in this group are advocating.
The people of this country are apprehensive about the future. The forces of reaction are already getting arrayed for a show-down after the war is over. The people realize that private enterprise, in spite of all the excess profits taxes that are being paid, is to-day

Social Security
being given control of Canadian industry, with its greatly increased plant and equipment, to a far greater extent than before the war. Newspapers, such as the famous one in the city from which I come, the Winnipeg Free Press, are doing their best to confuse the issue by idealizing the old order and using abusive language to describe the kind of economy which we in the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation advocate, a Canadian economy which the people will own and control so that there will be for all an income to enable every worker and every farmer to own his own home and to have for his very own the necessities of a good life.
The people are no longer disturbed or deceived by the old argument that socialism interferes with personal living and initiative and freedom. Socialism in fact is the only possible basis for full employment, for adequate incomes, for homes for everyone, for care of our health and real security in our old age. These things spell real freedom. These things make life worth living. These things inspire people to creative effort. These things draw out initiative. You cannot turn people away from their desire for these things by trying to tell them in this day and age that that is socialism. Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, these things are what democracy ought to be seeking to achieve. As I sit in this house and hear hon. members suggest that government should not interfere with the economic life of our country, I wonder what they were sent here for. I feel that I was sent here by the constituents I represent to work on their behalf, and definitely to seek in the name of the people to control and direct the economy of this country in such a way as to make possible good homes and a good life for the people of Winnipeg North Centre and of this entire country. I think it is our duty as members of this house to give our concern and deep thought to this whole question of controlling the economy of this country in the interests of the people that they may enjoy a good life.
I have urged upon the house the desirability of this committee giving its attention to our whole economy if it is going to establish a measure of social security that will be worth while. If I have hoped for too much, I hope that the committee will at least recommend the bringing down of legislation this session to increase old age pensions, to take care of our veterans and war widows, and put into effect a national programme for the health of our people. These things would give to our people a measure of confidence that when this war is over we are really going to have a better day.

maintopic: APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE ON NATIONAL SOCIAL INSURANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the predecessor of the last speaker (Mr. Knowles) representing Winnipeg North Centre occupied this seat when I first entered the house. I think we both entered on the same day. In those days we both had a resolution for social insurance, unemployment insurance and health insurance. Those resolutions went to a committee, just as it is proposed to send this question of social insurance, and what was the result?
It was found, in the first place, that owing to the constitution of Canada, dominion, provincial and municipal jurisdictions, such a scheme could not then be carried out; second, that the government of Canada, or any government, had no funds except what it raised from the taxpayers, and that to put such a scheme into effect the dominion would . have to come to the taxpayers to get the necessary funds, and the provinces would have to do the same thing and the municipalities the same.
We have come through two wars, and the taxpayer to-day has already pretty heavy burdens. The Beveridge report has been often referred to in this house; I have read it half a dozen times. Sir William Beveridge was a professor, a teacher at Oxford university. I do not see how it came about that the government of Great Britain took the action they did; for it is well known that a teacher or a professor is a theorist, not a practical man.
I have been a pioneer in this work for many years, Mr. Speaker, and I believe that the government of the day here is taking the wrong stand. We should- have, as they had in England, a two or three days' debate in the house on this subject to survey and chart a course of action. Recently I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to have a one day debate so that we might chart a course of what should be done about social security. In the first place there can be no security without, first of all, the returned soldiers having some security when they return. The first duty of parliament in any national scheme of insurance is to insure our soldiers, to take care of them and their dependents for three years after the war.
I have long advocated that, since the war began, by a resolution on the order paper, but nothing has been done about it. Nor can there be any security without an adequate housing scheme.. In England- the debate centred on housing. But nothing has been done to house our soldiers when they come home, or to house their dependents now. The armed forces can occupy mansion houses
United Nations Leaders

in the city from which I come, the old Flavelle property and one on Crescent road, for instance, while the soldiers' dependents have to live in cellars and all that kind of thing. Some cannot find a house. If this question of social security is referred to a committee of this house I believe that that will be the end of the whole question for this session.
As I shall require about ten or fifteen minutes more to finish, Mr. Speaker, I move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.

At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Thursday, March 4, 1943
